summary: The Erie harbor north pier light: a white iron tower at the end of Presque Isle's north pier, guarding the harbor entrance; moved along the pier in 1882, 1891 and 1940.

light.characteristic: fixed red 1882-1995; automated flashing red since 1995

access.note: Owned by the Coast Guard. Grounds open during Presque Isle State Park hours; tower closed to the public.

events.note: Congress appropriated $674 to complete the beacon-light at the pier end (LighthouseFriends)
Beacon and new sixth-order lens destroyed when a vessel struck the tower in a gale; the marker and the nonprofit page date the loss to 1857
Iron tower began operating; the marker gives 1858
Sixth-order Fresnel lens (USLHS)
Iron tower moved to the outer end of the pier
Fixed white changed to fixed red
Fourth-order lens installed, exchanged with Crossover Island (New York); 934-foot elevated walk built
North pier extended 450 feet; tower moved; move to within 30 feet of outer end recorded 10 October 1891
Iron tower moved again after the 1891 pier extension (LighthouseFriends)
Beacon moved about 20 feet from the outer end of the new pier extension
Ten-inch steam whistle on the peninsula fog-signal station began operating 1 August 1899
Keeper's dwelling rebuilt and enlarged for the families of two keepers
Keeper Robert Allen awarded silver medal of honor by the Life-Saving Service
Steamer Tempest sank in the channel near the station after her boilers blew up (August)
Keepers, assistants and keepers' wives credited with rescuing the Tempest crew
Lights electrified: fixed to occulting, oil changed to electric incandescent
Machine-operated bell changed to an air diaphone
Fire on the peninsula over several days; keepers Shaw and Allen fought it
Tyfon air signal replaced the fog bell on the pier
Tower moved to its present location and encased in steel plates
Class C radiobeacon established
Fourth-order Fresnel lens removed; lens sent to Erie Maritime Museum
Automated, solar-powered red flashing light installed
Coast Guard offered the tower as excess property under the National Historic Lighthouse Preservation Act (12 January 2023)

corrections.why: The USLHS place record gives the light 40.5 ft (12.3 m) above mean high water; the 8.2 m figure is not supported by the archive or by LighthouseFriends.

corrections.proposed: fourth-order Fresnel lens, on display at the Erie Maritime Museum
corrections.why: The record has no lens. LighthouseFriends says the fourth-order lens from 1883 is on display at the Erie Maritime Museum, and the nonprofit page says the Coast Guard removed it in 1995.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: Record and Wikidata say 1858. The USLHS place record and LighthouseFriends say the iron tower began operating in 1857; the Erie marker says it has guided mariners since 1858. The story uses 1857 and gives both.

Record says 1830 (Rowlett). The nonprofit page says the wooden tower was built in 1830, and the Board's 1837 appropriation refers to completing the beacon-light, so an earlier beacon is likely but the 1830 date is not confirmed by a Board report in the corpus.
LighthouseFriends dates the gale loss of the wooden beacon to 1855. The Erie marker and the nonprofit page say 1857.

Record lists moves in 1882 and 1940 only. The Board's report for the fiscal year ended 30 June 1892 records the 1891 move, and the 1894 report records another move of the beacon. LighthouseFriends dates the 1882 move to 1882; the nonprofit page says 1883.
Record and OSM say active; USLHS says inactive. The marker and the nonprofit page say the Coast Guard still operates an automated red flashing light, so the light is active.
The Board's 1899 report places the peninsula fog-signal station westerly of the pier beacon. LighthouseFriends says it lay about a mile and a half north.
The Board's report for the year ended 30 June 1901 gives 22 September 1900 for the color change to white. LighthouseFriends says 1901.
Record gives 10.4 m (34 ft, from Wikidata). LighthouseFriends gives 26.5 ft for the original tower. USLHS gives 32 ft from base to lantern centre. The figures are not reconciled here.

notes_for_editor: Pre-1891 dates rest mainly on LighthouseFriends, a secondary source, because the Board reports in the local corpus start in 1891 and Chronicling America returned no Pennsylvania hits for the pierhead in 1850-1925. Keeper rows come from the USLHS roster (NARA registers via the Kraig Anderson inventory) and were not checked against primary keeper records; the roster spells Leonard Vaughn where LighthouseFriends and the marker spell Vaughan. The roster's first entry (Samuel Foster, 1835-1836) predates the 1837 beacon that LighthouseFriends describes as just established; no source checked explains it. The 'will be extended 450 feet' passage is in the 1891 part of the bound 1891-1892 volume (annualreportlig03statgoog, scan p.188), so it is the report for the fiscal year ended 30 June 1891, not 1892. The 1899 fog-signal station direction (Board: westerly; LighthouseFriends: north) and the 1901 color-change date (Board: 22 Sept 1900; LighthouseFriends: 1901) disagree; the story states the direction disagreement. The 1924 change: the Bulletin list names only 'Presque Isle, Pa.' (bell operated by machinery to air diaphone); LighthouseFriends says the diaphone replaced the steam whistle on 6 Aug 1924. Not reconciled. The 1913 Bulletin entry places Robert Allen at 'Presque Isle Pierhead Light Station, N. Y.' (state wrong; Pennsylvania per LighthouseFriends and USLHS); the medal is matched by name and the Bulletin's own page 27. The 1918 index entries (Allen 36, 43; Owens 43; Huntington 43) were matched by name in the OCR index, and the Tempest passage is on PDF page 43 of the 1918 Bulletin. The 2023 transfer offer is reported by LighthouseFriends; a 2025 GoErie article (not readable: HTTP 403) reports a joining of the nonprofit with the light, and the outcome is not confirmed here. The nonprofit page dates the wooden tower to 1830 and the iron tower's move to 1883, so its dates are used only where marked. The Erie marker's cast-iron/France claim is repeated on the nonprofit page; no primary source was checked for it. Wikipedia was consulted for leads only and is not cited.
